title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs:
“Oh, sir, the loftiest hopes on earth
Draw lots with meaner hopes: heroic breasts,
Breathing bad air, run risk of pestilence;
Or, lacking lime-juice when they cross the Line,
May languish with the scurvy.”

Several weeks passed after this conversation before the chaplaincy became a practical concern for Lydgate. Without admitting why, he put off deciding how to vote. It would really have been a matter of complete indifference to him—meaning he would have chosen the convenient side and voted for Tyke without hesitation—if he had not personally cared for Mr. Farebrother.

But his affection for the Vicar of St. Botolph's increased as he knew him better. Understanding that Lydgate was a newcomer with professional aims of his own, Mr. Farebrother had taken pains to discourage rather than secure his support. This showed an unusual delicacy and generosity to which Lydgate was acutely sensitive. It accompanied other exceptionally fine qualities of conduct, making the Vicar's character resemble a southern landscape divided between natural grandeur and human untidiness. Few men could have shown such devoted and chivalrous care towards the mother, aunt, and sister whose dependence had shaped his life in many ways uncomfortable for himself. Few men pressed by small necessities are so nobly determined not to disguise their inevitably self-interested wishes as higher motives. In these matters he knew his life could bear the closest examination. Perhaps that knowledge encouraged a little defiance towards the strict criticism of people whose close relations with heaven did not seem to improve their manners at home, and whose actions required no lofty ambitions to explain them. His preaching, too, was inventive and concise, like the preaching of the English Church in its vigorous age, and he delivered his sermons without a text before him. People came from outside the parish to hear him. Since filling a church was always the hardest part of a clergyman's work, this gave him another reason for an easy sense of superiority. Besides, he was likable: good-tempered, quick-witted, and frank, without smiles of concealed bitterness or other conversational seasonings that make half of us a burden to our friends. Lydgate liked him wholeheartedly and wanted his friendship.

With this feeling uppermost, Lydgate kept setting the chaplaincy aside. He persuaded himself not only that it was none of his proper business, but that he probably would never be troubled by having to vote. At Mr. Bulstrode's request he was drawing up plans for the new hospital's internal arrangements, and the two often consulted together. The banker continually assumed that he could count on Lydgate's general cooperation, but did not specifically return to the approaching choice between Tyke and Farebrother. Then the Infirmary's General Board met, and Lydgate learned that the chaplaincy had been referred to a council of directors and medical men, to meet the following Friday. Irritated, he realized he must decide this trivial Middlemarch business. An unmistakable inward voice declared that Bulstrode was prime minister and the Tyke question meant holding office or losing it. Equally unmistakable was his dislike of surrendering the prospect of office. Everything he observed confirmed Mr. Farebrother's warning that the banker would not overlook opposition. “Damn their petty politics!” was one of his reflections during three mornings' shaving, as he began to feel he must truly bring the matter before the court of his conscience. There were certainly sound objections to choosing Mr. Farebrother. He already had too much to do, especially given the time he devoted to activities outside his clerical duties. And the Vicar's obvious interest in winning money at cards repeatedly jarred against Lydgate's respect for him. He enjoyed the game, certainly, but clearly also enjoyed something it paid for. Mr. Farebrother defended all games in principle and said Englishmen's wits stagnated for lack of them. Yet Lydgate was certain he would play much less without the money. The Green Dragon had a billiard room which some anxious mothers and wives considered Middlemarch's chief temptation. The Vicar was an excellent billiard player. He did not frequent the Green Dragon, but reports said he had sometimes visited by day and won money. Nor did he pretend to want the chaplaincy for anything except its forty pounds. Lydgate was no Puritan, but he did not enjoy gambling, and winning money that way had always seemed mean to him. Moreover, his ideal of life made him thoroughly dislike conduct governed by the pursuit of small sums. His own needs had always been supplied without effort on his part. His first instinct was to give half-crowns freely, as trifles beneath a gentleman's concern; he had never thought of devising a way to earn half-crowns. He had always known, generally, that he was not rich, but he had never felt poor. He could not imagine how lack of money directs men's actions. Money had never been his motive. He was therefore unwilling to excuse this deliberate pursuit of small gains. It repelled him altogether, and he never calculated the relation between the Vicar's income and his more or less unavoidable expenses. Possibly he would not have made that calculation even for himself.

Now that the vote approached, this repellent fact weighed more heavily against Mr. Farebrother than before. How much easier decisions would be if people's characters were more consistent, and particularly if our friends were always suited to whatever posts they wanted! Lydgate felt certain that, without a valid objection to Mr. Farebrother, he would have voted for him regardless of Bulstrode's feelings. He had no intention of becoming Bulstrode's dependent servant. On the other hand stood Tyke, wholly devoted to his clerical work, merely a curate at an outlying chapel in St. Peter's parish, and with time for additional duties. Nobody had anything against him except that they could not stand him and suspected his piety of being cant. From his own point of view, Bulstrode was thoroughly justified.

Yet whichever way Lydgate leaned, something made him wince. Being proud, he was irritated at having to wince at all. He disliked frustrating his best purposes by falling out with Bulstrode. He disliked voting against Farebrother and helping deprive him of work and income. Might not the extra forty pounds free the Vicar from that undignified concern with card winnings? Lydgate also disliked knowing that a vote for Tyke would favor the side most obviously convenient to himself. But would his own convenience really be the object? Others would say so. They would claim he was courting Bulstrode to increase his own importance and get ahead. What of it? He knew that, had only his personal prospects been involved, he would not have cared a rotten nut whether the banker was friend or enemy. What he really wanted was a setting for his work, a means of carrying out his ideas. Was he not, after all, obliged to put the creation of a good hospital, where he could demonstrate the distinctions between fevers and test treatments, ahead of every other consideration connected with the chaplaincy? For the first time he felt the restricting, threadlike pressure of small social circumstances and their frustrating complexity. When he finally set out for the hospital after this inward debate, he was really hoping the discussion might somehow put the question in a new light and tip the balance enough to spare him a vote. I think he also relied a little on the energy circumstances generate: some feeling might rush warmly through him and make resolution easy, where cool debate had only made it harder. Whatever the case, he did not clearly tell himself how he would vote. All the while he resented being forced into this dependence. Earlier it would have seemed absurdly illogical that a man with his uncompromising independence and chosen aims should find himself, at the very start, trapped between petty alternatives equally distasteful to him. In his student rooms he had planned his dealings with society quite differently.

Lydgate set out late, but Dr. Sprague, the other two surgeons, and several directors arrived early. Mr. Bulstrode, the treasurer and chairman, was still absent. Conversation suggested that the result remained uncertain; a majority for Tyke was less secure than people had assumed. Astonishingly, the two physicians were united—or rather, though they thought differently, they would act together. Dr. Sprague, solid and formidable, supported Mr. Farebrother, as everyone expected. The Doctor was strongly suspected of having no religion at all. Somehow Middlemarch tolerated that deficiency as if he were a Lord Chancellor. Indeed, people probably believed all the more in his professional authority. The ancient association of cleverness with the devil remained powerful, even among female patients with the strictest ideas about frills and proper feelings. Perhaps the Doctor's unbelief led his neighbors to call him hard-headed and dry-witted, qualities of texture also considered favorable for storing judgments about drugs. At any rate, a medical man arriving in Middlemarch with a reputation for definite religious opinions, frequent prayer, and other displays of active piety would certainly have faced a general suspicion of his medical skill.

In that respect Dr. Minchin was professionally fortunate that his religious sympathies were broad. They offered a distant medical blessing to all serious feeling, Anglican or Dissenting, rather than allegiance to particular doctrines. When Mr. Bulstrode insisted, as he often did, that the Lutheran doctrine of justification determined whether a Church stood or fell, Dr. Minchin replied that man was certainly no mere machine or accidental collection of atoms. When Mrs. Wimple insisted that Providence concerned itself particularly with her stomach complaint, Dr. Minchin liked to keep the windows of the mind open and opposed fixed boundaries. When the Unitarian brewer joked about the Athanasian Creed, Dr. Minchin quoted Pope's “Essay on Man.” He disliked Dr. Sprague's rather free style of anecdote, preferring respectable quotations and refinement of every kind. Everyone knew he was related to a bishop and sometimes spent his holidays at “the palace.”

With his soft hands, pale face, and rounded shape, Dr. Minchin could have passed for a gentle clergyman. Dr. Sprague, by contrast, was unnecessarily tall. His trousers creased at the knees and exposed too much boot in an age when trouser straps seemed essential to a dignified appearance. You could hear him entering, leaving, and going upstairs and down as if he had come to inspect the roof. In short, he had weight and could be expected to wrestle a disease to the ground. Dr. Minchin might be better at detecting it in hiding and outmaneuvering it. Both enjoyed the mysterious privilege of medical reputation in roughly equal measure, and concealed their contempt for each other's abilities behind elaborate etiquette. Considering themselves Middlemarch institutions, they were ready to unite against innovators and interfering laymen. On those grounds both privately disliked Mr. Bulstrode equally, although Dr. Minchin had never opposed him openly and never disagreed without explaining himself fully to Mrs. Bulstrode, who believed he alone understood her constitution. A layman who investigated doctors' professional conduct and continually thrust reforms upon them offended the profession's nostrils as such, even if he embarrassed the two physicians less directly than the surgeon-apothecaries contracted to treat paupers. Dr. Minchin fully shared the fresh irritation at Bulstrode's apparent determination to patronize Lydgate. The established practitioners, Mr. Wrench and Mr. Toller, stood apart in friendly conversation, agreeing that Lydgate was an upstart perfectly suited to Bulstrode's purposes. Among nonmedical friends they had already agreed in praising the other young practitioner who had arrived after Mr. Peacock's retirement. He brought no recommendation beyond his own merits and whatever evidence of solid professional knowledge could be inferred from his apparently having wasted no time on other subjects. Clearly, Lydgate's refusal to dispense medicines was intended to cast suspicion on his equals and blur the boundary between a general practitioner like himself and the physicians. In the profession's interests the physicians felt obliged to preserve its ranks, especially against a man who had attended neither English university and enjoyed their absence of anatomical and bedside teaching. Instead he came with a slanderous claim to experience in Edinburgh and Paris, where observation might be plentiful but could hardly be sound.

So on this occasion Bulstrode became identified with Lydgate, and Lydgate with Tyke. The chaplaincy question acquired several interchangeable names, allowing very different minds to reach the same conclusion.

As soon as he entered, Dr. Sprague bluntly told the assembled group, “I'm for Farebrother. A salary, by all means. But why take it away from the Vicar? He's hardly overpaid. He has to insure his life as well as maintain a household and meet a vicar's charitable obligations. Put forty pounds in his pocket and you'll do no harm. Farebrother's a good fellow, with just enough parson about him to remain in orders.”

“Ho, ho, Doctor!” said old Mr. Powderell, a retired ironmonger of some standing. His exclamation fell somewhere between a laugh and a parliamentary protest. “We must let you speak your mind. But the question isn't anybody's income. It's the souls of the poor sick people.” Genuine feeling showed in his voice and face. “Mr. Tyke truly preaches the Gospel. I'd be voting against my conscience if I voted against him. I really would.”

“I don't believe Mr. Tyke's opponents have asked anyone to vote against his conscience,” said Mr. Hackbutt, a wealthy and fluent tanner, turning his glittering spectacles and upright hair rather sternly towards the innocent Mr. Powderell. “But as Directors, we ought to consider whether our sole business is to carry out proposals coming from one particular quarter. Can any committee member claim that he would have thought of removing the gentleman who has always served as chaplain here, unless prompted by people inclined to treat every institution in this town as machinery for imposing their own opinions? I accuse no man's motives. Let those rest between himself and a higher Power. But I do say that influences are operating here which cannot coexist with true independence. Crawling servility is usually dictated by circumstances that those gentlemen who practice it could not afford, morally or financially, to admit. I am a layman myself, but I have paid considerable attention to divisions within the Church, and—”

“Oh, damn the divisions!” broke in Mr. Frank Hawley, the lawyer and town clerk. He seldom came to board meetings but had now hurried in, whip in hand. “They have nothing to do with us here. Farebrother has done the work—such as it was—for nothing. If there's going to be pay, he should get it. Taking the job away from him is a damned piece of favoritism.”
“Gentlemen might do better to avoid personal remarks,” said Mr. Plymdale. “I intend to vote for Mr. Tyke, but without Mr. Hackbutt's hint I wouldn't have known that made me a Servile Crawler.”
“I deny making personal remarks. I expressly said, if I may repeat myself, or even finish what I was about to say—”

“Ah, here's Minchin!” said Mr. Frank Hawley. Everyone turned away from Mr. Hackbutt, leaving him to feel how useless superior gifts were in Middlemarch. “Come, Doctor, you'll be on the right side, eh?”
“I hope so,” said Dr. Minchin, nodding and shaking hands around the room, “whatever it costs my feelings.”
“If feelings come into it,” said Mr. Frank Hawley, “they ought to be for the man being turned out.”

“I admit I also have feelings on the other side. My esteem is divided,” said Dr. Minchin, rubbing his hands. “I consider Mr. Tyke exemplary—no man more so—and believe the motives for proposing him are beyond reproach. Personally, I wish I could vote for him. But my view of the case obliges me to give greater weight to Mr. Farebrother's claims. He is an agreeable man, a capable preacher, and has been among us longer.”
Old Mr. Powderell watched sadly without speaking. Mr. Plymdale adjusted his cravat uneasily.

“I hope you're not presenting Farebrother as a model clergyman,” said Mr. Larcher, the prominent carrier, who had just entered. “I've no ill will towards him, but in these appointments we owe something to the public, quite apart from anything higher. I find Farebrother too lax for a clergyman. I don't want to list particular charges, but he'll make as little attendance here as possible serve the purpose.”

“And a damned sight better than too much,” said Mr. Hawley, whose language was notorious in that part of the county. “Sick people can't stand all that praying and preaching. That Methodist sort of religion lowers the spirits—bad for the insides, eh?” He turned briskly to the four assembled medical men.

No answer was needed, because three more gentlemen entered and received greetings of varying warmth: the Reverend Edward Thesiger, rector of St. Peter's; Mr. Bulstrode; and our friend Mr. Brooke of Tipton. Mr. Brooke had recently agreed to take his turn on the board of directors but had never attended before. His presence now was due to Mr. Bulstrode's efforts. Only Lydgate was still expected.

Everyone sat down, with Mr. Bulstrode presiding, pale and controlled as usual. Mr. Thesiger, a moderate Evangelical, advocated his friend Mr. Tyke's appointment. Tyke was zealous and capable, and his duties at an outlying chapel did not involve so many souls that he lacked ample time for the new responsibility. Such chaplaincies should be undertaken with fervent purpose; they offered exceptional opportunities for spiritual influence. Although a salary was desirable, it made careful vigilance still more necessary, lest the position become merely a matter of pay. Mr. Thesiger spoke with such quiet propriety that his opponents could only simmer silently.

Mr. Brooke believed everyone meant well. He had not personally attended to the Infirmary's affairs, though he felt deeply interested in everything that benefited Middlemarch and was delighted to meet the gentlemen present over any public question. “Any public question, you know,” he repeated, nodding with perfect understanding. “My work as a magistrate keeps me rather busy, along with gathering documentary evidence. But I consider my time at the public's disposal. And, in short, my friends have persuaded me that a chaplain with a salary—a salary, you know—is an excellent thing. I'm glad to come here and vote to appoint Mr. Tyke, whom I understand to be entirely suitable, apostolic and eloquent and all that sort of thing. I'm the last man to withhold my vote, under the circumstances, you know.”

“It sounds as if you've been fed only one side of the question, Mr. Brooke,” said Mr. Frank Hawley. He feared nobody and, as a Tory, suspected electioneering motives. “You don't appear to know that one of our worthiest men has served here as chaplain for years without pay, and that Mr. Tyke is being proposed to replace him.”
“Excuse me, Mr. Hawley,” said Mr. Bulstrode. “Mr. Brooke has been fully informed about Mr. Farebrother's character and situation.”
“By his enemies,” Mr. Hawley snapped.
“I hope no personal hostility enters into this,” said Mr. Thesiger.
“I'll swear it does,” Mr. Hawley retorted.

“Gentlemen,” said Mr. Bulstrode quietly, “the merits can be stated very briefly. If anyone doubts that every gentleman about to vote has been fully informed, I can now summarize the considerations on both sides.”

“I see no point,” said Mr. Hawley. “I assume we all know whom we're voting for. A man who wants to be fair doesn't wait until the last moment to hear both sides. I've no time to waste. I propose we vote immediately.”
A short but heated discussion followed. Then each man wrote “Tyke” or “Farebrother” on a slip of paper and dropped it into a drinking glass. Meanwhile, Mr. Bulstrode saw Lydgate arrive.
“I find the votes are at present evenly divided,” said Mr. Bulstrode in a clear, cutting voice. He looked up at Lydgate.
“One deciding vote remains. It is yours, Mr. Lydgate. Would you kindly write it down?”
“That settles it,” said Mr. Wrench, getting up. “We all know how Mr. Lydgate will vote.”
“You seem to attach some particular meaning to that, sir,” said Lydgate rather defiantly, holding his pencil still.
“Only that you're expected to vote with Mr. Bulstrode. Do you find that meaning offensive?”
“Others may. But that won't stop me voting with him.” Lydgate immediately wrote “Tyke.”

And so the Reverend Walter Tyke became the Infirmary's chaplain, and Lydgate continued working with Mr. Bulstrode. He genuinely doubted whether Tyke might not be the better candidate. Yet he knew inwardly that, without indirect influences, he would have voted for Mr. Farebrother. The chaplaincy remained a painful memory, an occasion on which Middlemarch's petty social environment had proved too strong for him. How could anyone be satisfied with a choice between such alternatives in such circumstances? No more than with a hat chosen from the shapes the age happens to offer. At best he wears it with a resignation supported chiefly by comparison.

Mr. Farebrother, however, greeted him with the same friendliness as before. In practice, the character of a publican and sinner is not always incompatible with that of a modern Pharisee. Most of us see our own faulty behavior little more clearly than our faulty reasoning or dull jokes. But the Vicar of St. Botolph's had certainly escaped even the faintest taint of the Pharisee. By admitting to himself that he was all too much like other men, he had become remarkably unlike them in one respect: he could forgive others for thinking poorly of him, and judge their conduct fairly even when it worked against him.

“I know the world has proved too strong for ME,” he told Lydgate one day. “But I'm no mighty man. I'll never be famous. Hercules choosing between virtue and pleasure makes a pretty fable, but Prodicus gives the hero an easy task, as though the first resolutions were enough. Another story has him end up holding a woman's distaff, and finally wearing the poisoned shirt of Nessus. I suppose one good resolution might keep a man on course if everyone else's resolution helped him.”

The Vicar's conversation was not always encouraging. He had escaped becoming a Pharisee, but not the low estimate of what is possible that we rather hastily infer from our own failures. Lydgate thought Mr. Farebrother suffered from a pitiable weakness of will.
